name: PCF8574T_3,518
title: PCF8574 / PCF8574A: 8-bit quasi-bidirectional I/O port expander on I2C
summary: A CMOS slave on the two-wire I2C bus that gives a controller eight extra port lines. Each line is quasi-bidirectional: it is written as a latched output or, once set HIGH, read as an input, with no direction register. An open-drain INT output goes LOW when any input changes, telling the controller of new port data without bus traffic. Three address pins give eight addresses; the PCF8574A answers on a second block of eight, so sixteen can share one bus. It runs from 2.5 V to 6 V and the SCL clock reaches 100 kHz.

circuits.title: Several PCF8574s on one interrupt line
circuits.description: The open-drain INT outputs of up to sixteen expanders join on one wire to the controller's interrupt input, held HIGH by a single resistor to VDD. Any expander whose inputs change pulls the wire LOW, signalling the controller without any bus traffic.
notes: Expanders 3 to 15 join the INT wire the same way as U2, U3 and U4.

equations.name: Slave address byte

where.R/W: 1 to read the port, 0 to write it

equations.note: The first bit sent after START is the leftmost.

operation.text: SDA and SCL each need a pull-up resistor to the positive supply; both sit HIGH while the bus is idle, and a transfer may only begin then. SDA holds still while SCL is HIGH and changes only while SCL is LOW; an SDA edge during SCL HIGH is a control signal: falling is START (S), rising is STOP (P). The master drives the clock and starts and ends each message; the PCF8574 is always a slave.

Every byte is eight bits followed by a ninth, acknowledge, clock that the master generates. During it the transmitter releases SDA and the receiver pulls SDA LOW and holds it through the HIGH part of that clock, observing set-up and hold times. An addressed slave acknowledges each byte it receives. When reading, the master acknowledges every byte except the last; leaving that one unacknowledged tells the slave to release SDA so the master can send STOP. Any number of bytes may pass between START and STOP.

After START the master sends the 7-bit slave address and the R/W bit. The upper four address bits are fixed (0100 on the PCF8574, 0111 on the PCF8574A) and A2, A1, A0 are the levels on the three address pins, so up to eight of each type, sixteen in all, can sit on one bus. The two types are otherwise identical.

With R/W = 0, each byte the master sends after the address is latched onto P7 to P0, and the port lines take the new value within tpv after the acknowledge clock that ends the byte. Further bytes update the port the same way until STOP.

With R/W = 1, the PCF8574 returns the state of P7 to P0 in each byte, sampling the port at the acknowledge clock that precedes the byte; input data must be set up tsu before and held th after that point. The master ends the read by not acknowledging the last byte and sending STOP. A STOP may end a transfer at any moment: the output data latched at the last acknowledge stays valid on the port, and input data not yet read is lost.

INT is an open-drain output that goes LOW within tiv after a port line used as an input changes level in either direction. It is released, and the interrupt logic re-armed, when the port returns to its earlier state or when the expander that raised it is read or written; a read clears it at the acknowledge bit once SCL has risen, a write at the acknowledge bit once SCL has fallen, within tir. A change that occurs during the acknowledge clock can be lost or give only a very short pulse. Once cleared, each new change is caught and appears on INT following the next SCL rising edge. Traffic to other devices on the bus leaves the interrupt untouched. Many INT outputs may be wired together on one pull-up.

Each port line is an open-drain pull-down plus a weak current source (about 100 µA, IOH 30 to 300 µA) to VDD, with no direction control. Writing a 1 leaves only the current source on, and the line can then be driven LOW from outside and read as an input; a line must be written HIGH before it is used as an input. For a fast rising edge into a heavy load, a strong pull-up to VDD turns on briefly when a line is written HIGH (IOHt, about 1 mA at VDD = 2.5 V) and turns off at the next falling SCL edge. The LOW side sinks 25 mA typical, enough to drive an LED directly.
Below VPOR (1.3 V typ, 2.4 V max) the I2C logic is held in reset and every port line is set to 1 with its current source on, so all lines come up HIGH.
The inputs and outputs carry ESD protection for normal handling; the usual precautions for MOS devices apply.
